query: For high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what testable methodological hypothesis could enable improved combinations of strength, ductility, Young’s modulus, and fracture resistance? Explain why it should work, what measurable improvement is expected relative to the state of the art, the conditions under which it should or should not hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an experimental result that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Hybrid thermo-mechanical processing combining cryo-rolling followed by warm-rolling and short annealing (800 °C for 1 hour) in an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will generate a heterogeneous nanostructure with retained deformed regions and recrystallized zones, resulting in improved strength (by ~15-20%), ductility (by ~10%), and enhanced Young’s modulus and fracture resistance compared with conventional processing.
generation.material_initial_state: Cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA with inherited lamellar microstructure.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to severe cryo-rolling (e.g., 90% thickness reduction) followed by warm-rolling (to utilize stored deformation energy) and annealing at 800 °C for 1 hour.
generation.conditions: Processing must be performed with controlled rolling reductions and holding times in inert atmosphere; the hybrid process is effective if the stored energy from cryo-rolling accelerates controlled recrystallization during warm-rolling and annealing.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a dual heterogeneous nanostructure with distinct recrystallized ultrafine grains and retained deformed regions enriched in finely dispersed nano-precipitates.
generation.mechanism: The heterogeneous microstructure generates strain gradients and geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) that produce long-range back-stresses, delaying necking and crack initiation while promoting work-hardening.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to alloys processed by typical room-temperature rolling, yield strength is expected to increase by roughly 15-20% and uniform elongation by about 10%, with improved modulus and higher fracture toughness owing to the robust microstructural interfaces.
generation.baseline: Alloy processed by standard cold-rolling and annealing with more homogeneous microstructure.
generation.boundary: If the hybrid processing leads to over-refinement or triggers unwanted excessive precipitation, the improvements may not manifest.
generation.uncertainty: The optimization of rolling temperatures, reduction ratios, and annealing times is critical; minor deviations may lead to suboptimal phase distributions.

falsification_experiment.design: Process AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA samples with both the hybrid cryo-/warm-rolling route and a standard cold-rolling route; characterize microstructures (TEM, EBSD) and perform mechanical tests (tensile, fracture toughness).
measurements: Grain size and heterogeneity assessment (TEM, EBSD)
Young’s modulus and fracture toughness measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the hybrid processed samples do not demonstrate the predicted relative improvements in strength, ductility, and fracture resistance (i.e. less than a 10-15% improvement relative to standard processing) or lack the predicted heterogeneous microstructure, the hypothesis must be rejected.

cited_evidence.text: Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism. This work provides a pathway for strengthening eutectic alloys and widens the design toolbox for high-performance materials based upon EHEAs. While the extreme strength in the hybrid-processed EHEA is contributed by various strengthening mechanisms including nanostructuring and presence of hard B2 phase and nano-precipitates. The outstanding strength-ductility combination of the hybrid-rolled EHEA originates from the extreme heterogeneities. It is perceived that in heterogeneous materials, mechanical incompatibility between the different domains results in the development of strain gradients near the interfaces or domain boundaries, which must be accommodated by geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs),. The pile up of GNDs at the interfaces/domain boundaries leads to the development of long-range back stress which increases with the increasing strain, eventually leading to back-stress strengthening. papers.title: Multi-Phase Design Strategy for Synergistic Strength-Ductility Optimization in V-Ti-Cr-Nb-Mo Refractory High-Entropy Alloys.
papers.approach: Systematic variation of elemental ratios and use of annealing treatments to produce dual‐phase (BCC + HCP) and triple‐phase (BCC + HCP + Laves) microstructures.
papers.findings: Demonstrated that tailored phase control via composition adjustment and subsequent heat treatments can significantly balance strength and ductility. For example, an as-cast triple‐phase alloy showed high compressive strength (up to 1775 MPa) with moderate ductility, while annealing led to grain coarsening and improved ductility at a slight cost to strength.
papers.mechanism: The interplay of multiple phases – each contributing differently (e.g., ductile BCC/HCP phases and strengthening Laves phase) – creates internal constraints and dislocation pinning which enhances the overall mechanical synergy.

papers.title: Microstructural Evolution and Tensile Properties of Al0.3CoCrFeNi High-Entropy Alloy Associated with B2 Precipitates.
papers.approach: Thermo-mechanical processing (cold rolling to various reductions followed by annealing) to adjust recrystallization and precipitate formation (notably B2 precipitates).
papers.findings: Processing led to variable microstructures – while 90% cold rolling and annealing at moderate temperatures produced ultrafine grains with B2 precipitates, resulting in an excellent strength–ductility balance (yield strengths around 800 MPa with ~40% uniform elongation).
papers.mechanism: The formation of coherent B2 precipitates and partial recrystallization creates grain boundary pinning and back-stress effects, which improve both strength and ductility.

papers.title: Enhanced strength-ductility synergy in ultrafine-grained eutectic high-entropy alloys by inheriting microstructural lamellae.
papers.approach: Tailored thermo-mechanical processing to deliberately preserve and inherit the casting-derived lamellar microstructure, then refine it into an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure.
papers.findings: Achieved a unique two-level heterogeneous structure that provides a synergy of high strength (exceeding previously reported values) and ductility by capitalizing on inherent lamellar architectures.
papers.mechanism: The inherited lamellar (duplex) structure contributes to a two-hierarchical constraint effect and facilitates a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism, which delays fracture and accommodates deformation.

papers.title: High-content ductile coherent nanoprecipitates achieve ultrastrong high-entropy alloys.
papers.system: HEAs with an FCC matrix reinforced by ductile, coherent nanoprecipitates
papers.approach: Controlling the volume fraction and coherence of ductile precipitates via precise alloying and processing design.
papers.findings: Produced HEAs with yield strengths tunable between ~270–1900 MPa while maintaining ductility (>40%) and work-hardening capacity, outperforming systems with non-coherent or lower content precipitates.
papers.mechanism: Ductile, low-misfit precipitates operate as effective obstacles to dislocation motion without compromising plasticity, leading to simultaneous improvements in strength and ductility.

papers.title: Nanostructuring with Structural-Compositional Dual Heterogeneities Enhances Strength-Ductility Synergy in Eutectic High Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA with engineered dual heterogeneities
papers.approach: Hybrid processing routes (combining severe deformation and controlled annealing) to produce networked dual heterogeneities in both structure and composition.
papers.findings: The resulting heterogeneous microstructure produces an exceptionally high strength-ductility combination by effectively introducing strain gradients and generating back-stress during deformation.
papers.mechanism: Heterogeneous domains and engineered compositional variations lead to the generation of geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) that create long-range back stress, delaying localization and necking.

papers.title: Vermicular Eutectic Multi-Principal Element Alloy with Exceptional Strength and Ductility.
papers.system: Eutectic multi‐principal element alloy (EMPEA) based on (AlCrFe2)65Ni35
papers.approach: Inducing a novel vermicular (kinked) eutectic microstructure via phase-field simulation guided design and adjusted processing to deviate from conventional rod-like/lamellar patterns.
papers.findings: The formation of a vermicular microstructure dramatically enhanced strength–ductility synergy, surpassing both coarse-grained and typical straight morphology alloys.
papers.mechanism: The kinked morphology, attributed to weak interphase anisotropy (matching elastic moduli of the two phases), results in improved load distribution and reduced stress concentrations.

papers.title: Heterogeneous precipitation mediated heterogeneous nanostructure enhances strength-ductility synergy in severely cryo-rolled and annealed CoCrFeNi HEA.
papers.system: CoCrFeNi-based HEA with minor Nb addition
papers.approach: Utilizing severe cryo-rolling to refine the microstructure, followed by annealing to create a heterogeneous distribution of nano-precipitates and retain deformed regions.
papers.findings: The cryo-rolled and annealed material exhibited a markedly enhanced combination of strength and ductility as compared to conventionally cold-rolled samples, due to a finer lamellar nanostructure and fragmentation of intermetallic phases.
papers.mechanism: Accelerated nucleation of fine precipitates in a cryo-deformed state promotes a heterogeneous microstructure that both inhibits recrystallization and generates a high density of strengthening obstacles while maintaining ductility.

papers.title: Effects of Heat Treatment on the Microstructure and Mechanical Properties of a Dual-Phase High-Entropy Alloy Fabricated via Laser Beam Power Bed Fusion.
papers.system: Dual-phase Fe32Cr33Ni29Al3Ti3 HEA produced via LB-PBF
papers.approach: Systematic post-processing heat treatments (varying temperature and cooling methods) to tune the phase fractions and grain size distribution in FCC/BCC dual-phase alloys.
papers.findings: Heat treatment (e.g., 1000 °C for 1 h with water cooling) lowered tensile and yield strength somewhat but significantly improved ductility (with elongations rising from <6% to ~13%), attributed to the emergence of a bimodal grain structure.
papers.mechanism: A dual-scale grain structure, where ultrafine grains contribute to strength while coarser grains promote ductility, combined with control over phase content, yields an optimized strength-ductility trade-off.

papers.title: Enhanced strength and ductility in a friction stir processing engineered dual phase high entropy alloy.
papers.system: Fe50Mn30Co10Cr10 HEA (exhibiting TRIP behavior with FCC and h.c.p phases)
papers.approach: Friction Stir Processing (FSP) to induce grain refinement and adjust phase fractions, thereby engineering a dual-phase microstructure with enhanced transformation-induced effects.
papers.findings: FSP resulted in a more uniform dispersion of the f.c.c. to h.c.p. transformation zones, stabilizing the TRIP effect and leading to simultaneous gains in strength and ductility.
papers.mechanism: Grain size reduction enhances phase stability while the controlled transformation (TRIP) promotes continuous work hardening and delays necking, ultimately improving the mechanical performance.

papers.title: Negative enthalpy alloys and local chemical ordering: a concept and route leading to synergy of strength and ductility.
papers.system: Negative enthalpy refractory HEAs with engineered local chemical ordering (LCO)
papers.approach: Designing alloys with engineered negative enthalpy to promote the formation of local chemical ordering during solid solution processing.
papers.findings: The resulting alloys exhibited superior strength (e.g., yield strength ~1160 MPa) and ductility (~24.5%) as the LCO promoted dislocation cross-slip and sustainable strain hardening.
papers.mechanism: Local chemical ordering creates a sub-nanometer to nanoscale structural modulation that alters dislocation motion, enhancing their interaction and accumulation, thereby achieving an effective synergy between strength and ductility.

papers.title: Strengthening in multi-principal element alloys with local-chemical-order roughened dislocation pathways.
papers.system: FCC NiCoCr medium-entropy alloy (MEA) and related HEAs
papers.approach: Atomistic modeling to study the effects of variable local chemical ordering on dislocation slip paths and obstacles.
papers.findings: Showed that spatial variations in stacking fault energy and local antiphase boundary energies due to LCO lead to non-uniform, roughened dislocation pathways which elevate the lattice resistance to dislocation motion.
papers.mechanism: The presence of multi-principal elements and adjustable LCO creates a rugged energy landscape, thereby tailoring the dislocation activation process and contributing to overall strengthening.

papers.title: Interstitial atoms enable joint twinning and transformation induced plasticity in strong and ductile high-entropy alloys.
papers.system: Interstitially alloyed HEAs (e.g., carbon-added systems) exhibiting TRIP and TWIP effects
papers.approach: Introducing interstitial elements to simultaneously facilitate nano-twinning and strain-induced phase transformation while preserving the f.c.c. matrix stability.
papers.findings: Compared with traditional substitutional HEAs, the interstitial alloyed system showed enhanced strength and ductility, highlighted by early onset nano-twinning and a moderated TRIP effect.
papers.mechanism: Interstitial atoms stabilize the parent phase and promote the formation of twin boundaries, while also modifying stacking fault energies to assist the TRIP mechanism, leading to joint contributions from both twinning-induced and transformation-induced plasticity.

papers.title: Microstructure and Mechanical Properties of Intergranular Boride Precipitation-Toughened HfMoNbTaTiZr Refractory High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: HfMoNbTaTiZr refractory HEA with minor boron addition
papers.approach: Incorporating a small amount of boron to induce the precipitation of intergranular borides with the aim of reinforcing grain boundary cohesion.
papers.findings: The presence of boride precipitates enhanced grain boundary strength, leading to improved work hardenability and alleviation of intergranular fracture, thus achieving better toughness in an otherwise brittle BCC matrix.
papers.mechanism: The formation of borides along the grain boundaries physically impedes crack propagation and enhances the cohesive strength at interfaces, thereby improving overall fracture resistance.

papers.title: Phase-transition assisted mechanical behavior of TiZrHfTax high-entropy alloys.
papers.approach: Altering Ta content to destabilize the bcc phase in favor of hcp precipitation, thus influencing the ductility-strength balance.
papers.findings: Lower Ta concentrations softens the bcc matrix which promotes ductility, while the emergent nearly isotropic hcp precipitates contribute to strengthening, yielding a beneficial dual-phase system.
papers.mechanism: The controlled phase transition (bcc to hcp) modulates the mechanical response by combining a ductile matrix with strengthening precipitates, effectively tuning the alloy's response to stress.

established: Multi-phase and dual-phase microstructures in HEAs can synergistically enhance strength and ductility.
Thermo-mechanical processing (e.g., rolling, annealing, cryo-rolling, friction stir processing) significantly influences microstructural refinement and phase distribution.
Local chemical ordering and controlled nanoprecipitation are crucial factors in overcoming the traditional strength–ductility trade-off.
Heterogeneous microstructures that produce strain gradients and back-stress effects can improve not only strength and ductility but have implications for fracture resistance.

approaches_tried.approach: Elemental composition tuning and heat treatment to control phase formation (dual/triple-phase design).
approaches_tried.outcome: Enhanced synergy between strength and ductility in refractory HEAs; however, trade-offs exist depending on phase fractions and precipitate sizes.

approaches_tried.approach: Thermo-mechanical processing including cold rolling, cryo-rolling, and friction stir processing.
approaches_tried.outcome: Achieved ultrafine grains, increased precipitate coherence, and enhanced TRIP/TWIP effects, resulting in improved mechanical properties with some sensitivity to processing conditions.

approaches_tried.approach: Engineering novel microstructures (e.g., inherited lamellae, vermicular eutectic patterns).
approaches_tried.outcome: Unlocked new property combinations (e.g., superior strength–ductility synergy) by breaking conventional straight-lamella constraints.

approaches_tried.approach: Utilizing local chemical ordering and interstitial alloying to modulate deformation mechanisms.
approaches_tried.outcome: Improved strain hardening and dislocation interactions, leading to a balanced enhancement of strength and ductility.

mechanisms: Precipitation strengthening via coherent, ductile nanoprecipitates.
Back-stress generation through heterogeneous microstructures and strain gradients.
Transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) and twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP) mechanisms.
Local chemical ordering (LCO) altering dislocation motion pathways and promoting cross-slip.
Phase-transformation control (e.g., bcc to hcp) to modulate ductility and yield behavior.
disagreements: The relative contribution of precipitation strengthening versus grain boundary or transformation-induced mechanisms is debated in different studies.
Variations exist in the interpretation of the optimal processing conditions to balance recrystallization and nanoscale precipitation.
Some reports indicate that the effect of precipitates on strength may be minor, suggesting that grain size effects or back-stress contributions dominate.
open_questions: How can processing conditions be simultaneously optimized to achieve improved combinations of strength, ductility, Young’s modulus, and fracture resistance?
What is the quantitative role of local chemical ordering versus traditional nanoprecipitation in controlling the overall mechanical response?
Under what conditions do specific phase interactions (e.g., ductile vs. brittle phases) maximize energy absorption and delay fracture?
How do microstructural heterogeneities at different length scales interact to influence Young’s modulus and fracture toughness?
opportunities: Investigate hybrid thermo-mechanical processing routes (e.g., combining cryo-rolling with controlled warm rolling) to fine-tune heterogeneous dual-phase microstructures.
Explore negative enthalpy alloying strategies and controlled interstitial additions to promote beneficial local chemical ordering.
Study the effects of innovative microstructural designs, such as vermicular eutectic structures, on not just strength and ductility but also on modulus and fracture resistance.

Implement combinatorial experiments that vary composition, processing, and heat-treatment conditions to decisively map the impact of multi-scale heterogeneities on the full suite of mechanical properties.

directions.direction: Tailored composition design to induce a controlled multi‐phase microstructure (e.g. dual or triple-phase combining BCC, HCP, and intermetallic phases) that promotes internal dislocation pinning and back‐stress effects.
directions.assessment: Directly targets the strength/ductility trade-off by exploiting phase coexistence. It is supported by multiple studies (e.g. PMC12156277, PMC6105605) showing that triple‐phase microstructures can create a synergistic blend of strength, ductility, and fracture resistance. The physics of dislocation motion impediment in multiphase alloys is well established, and the approach is feasible through composition tuning and controlled annealing.

directions.direction: Hybrid thermo‐mechanical processing (e.g. combining cryo-rolling with warm rolling and targeted annealing) to create heterogeneous micro/nanostructures with retained deformed regions and refined grains.
directions.assessment: This method directly addresses not only strength and ductility but also improves Young’s modulus uniformity and fracture resistance by generating strain gradients and back‐stress through heterogeneity. Prior evidence from PMC6687781 and PMC6353877 supports the idea. The processing appears challenging but feasible and would provide clear microstructural mediators.

directions.direction: Utilize negative enthalpy alloying to promote engineered local chemical ordering (LCO) in solid solutions.
directions.assessment: The formation of LCO can tailor dislocation slip and work hardening as supported by PMC10890820 and PMC6687833. This mechanism is attractive because it modulates the intrinsic lattice resistance and can lead to improvements in both stiffness (Young’s modulus) and fracture toughness. Its feasibility depends on careful alloying and low-temperature treatments.

directions.direction: Introduce interstitial atoms (e.g. carbon) to activate joint TRIP-TWIP mechanisms, enhancing nano-twinning and transformation-induced plasticity while stabilizing the matrix.
directions.assessment: This approach leverages the beneficial contributions of interstitials to trigger additional deformation mechanisms. Evidence from PMC5227964 and PMC12279185 indicates that interstitial alloying can enhance both strength and ductility. The method is directly testable and predicted to impact fracture resistance by delaying crack propagation via abundant twin boundaries.

directions.direction: Surface modification or coating strategies to locally reinforce grain boundaries and impede crack propagation.
directions.assessment: While not discussed in detail in the provided evidence, strengthening grain boundaries via coatings can, in principle, improve fracture resistance and maintain ductility. However, it is less directly related to the bulk combination of properties (strength, ductility, Young’s modulus) than the other approaches and thus is less promising compared with the above.

candidates.hypothesis: In a V-Ti-Cr-Nb-Mo refractory high-entropy alloy, tailoring the elemental ratios to induce a triple-phase microstructure (BCC + HCP + Laves) via composition adjustment and annealing at 1200 °C for 8 hours will result in a significant improvement in strength, ductility, Young’s modulus, and fracture resistance relative to the as-cast alloy.
candidates.intervention: Adjust the alloy composition to, for example, V15Ti30Cr5Nb35Mo15 followed by annealing at 1200 °C for 8 hours to promote the formation of a triple-phase (BCC + HCP + Laves) structure.

candidates.hypothesis: Hybrid thermo-mechanical processing combining cryo-rolling followed by warm-rolling and short annealing (800 °C for 1 hour) in an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will generate a heterogeneous nanostructure with retained deformed regions and recrystallized zones, resulting in improved strength (by ~15-20%), ductility (by ~10%), and enhanced Young’s modulus and fracture resistance compared with conventional processing.
candidates.intervention: Subject the alloy to severe cryo-rolling (e.g., 90% thickness reduction) followed by warm-rolling (to utilize stored deformation energy) and annealing at 800 °C for 1 hour.

candidates.hypothesis: Introducing alloying elements that promote negative enthalpy and local chemical ordering (LCO) in a refractory HEA, followed by low-temperature annealing (around 900 °C for 2 hours), will create sub-nanometer to nanoscale LCO regions that enhance dislocation cross-slip and work hardening, resulting in a balanced increase in yield strength (~10-15% improvement), ductility (~10% improvement), and a higher, more uniform Young’s modulus compared with a purely random solid solution.
candidates.intervention: Adjust the alloy composition (for example by tweaking Al, Ti, or similar elements) to achieve a negative mixing enthalpy regime and conduct a controlled low-temperature annealing at 900 °C for 2 hours to induce local chemical ordering.

candidates.hypothesis: Adding a controlled small amount (~0.5-1 wt%) of carbon as an interstitial element into a CoCrFeNi-based HEA, followed by controlled cold rolling and annealing at 750 °C for 1 hour, will activate simultaneous TRIP and TWIP mechanisms, thereby enhancing both strength and ductility (with a targeted improvement of ~15% in both yield strength and uniform elongation) and increasing fracture resistance via the formation of abundant, fine twin boundaries.
candidates.intervention: Introduce a low level of carbon (~0.5-1 wt%) during melting, then perform standard cold rolling (e.g. 70-90% reduction) followed by an annealing treatment at 750 °C for 1 hour.

candidates.hypothesis: Hybrid thermo-mechanical processing combining cryo-rolling followed by warm-rolling and short annealing (800 °C for 1 hour) in an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will generate a heterogeneous nanostructure with retained deformed regions and recrystallized zones, resulting in improved strength (by ~15-20%), ductility (by ~10%), and enhanced Young’s modulus and fracture resistance compared with conventional processing.
candidates.intervention: Subject the alloy to severe cryo-rolling (e.g., 90% thickness reduction) followed by warm-rolling (to utilize stored deformation energy) and annealing at 800 °C for 1 hour.

candidates.hypothesis: Hybrid thermo-mechanical processing combining cryo-rolling with well-controlled reduction steps (e.g. 90% thickness reduction with specified cryo-cooling rates) followed by warm-rolling and a precisely timed annealing at 800 °C for 1 hour will generate a heterogeneous nanostructure in an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA, leading to a ~15-20% increase in yield strength, ~10% improvement in uniform ductility, enhanced Young’s modulus, and higher fracture resistance compared with conventional room-temperature rolling.
candidates.intervention: Subject the alloy to severe cryo-rolling with a controlled 90% thickness reduction using specific rolling speeds and cooling rates, followed immediately by warm-rolling using stored deformation energy, then perform annealing at 800 °C for 1 hour in an inert atmosphere.
candidates.changes: Expanded details of the processing parameters and optimization challenges; added specification of precise reduction steps and cooling rates to ensure reproducible formation of the heterogeneous nanostructure.

candidates.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled amount (0.5–1 wt%) of interstitial carbon into a CoCrFeNi-based HEA, followed by cold rolling with a reduction of 70–90% and annealing at 750 °C for 1 hour using a fast heating/cooling schedule, will activate simultaneous TRIP and TWIP mechanisms, thereby achieving approximately a 15% enhancement in yield strength and uniform elongation along with increased fracture resistance compared to the carbon-free HEA.
candidates.intervention: Add 0.5–1 wt% carbon during melting to ensure a uniform interstitial distribution, then apply cold rolling (70–90% reduction) followed by a controlled annealing treatment at 750 °C for 1 hour with rapid heating and cooling to minimize carbide precipitation.
candidates.changes: Clarified the rationale for the specified carbon content, added details to mitigate carbide formation by prescribing time–temperature processing windows, and provided clearer baseline references for mechanical property improvements.

candidates.hypothesis: Tailoring the elemental ratios in a V-Ti-Cr-Nb-Mo refractory HEA to promote a triple-phase microstructure (BCC + HCP + Laves) by using a composition such as V15Ti30Cr5Nb35Mo15 followed by annealing at 1200 °C for 8 hours will result in a ~10-20% improvement in yield and compressive strength, a 5-10% increase in ductility, and enhanced fracture resistance relative to the as-cast dual-phase alloy.
candidates.intervention: Adjust the alloy composition (e.g. V15Ti30Cr5Nb35Mo15) to favor the formation of secondary phases and then anneal the alloy at 1200 °C for 8 hours in an inert atmosphere to induce a triple-phase decomposition (BCC + HCP + Laves).
candidates.changes: Provided more detailed justification based on thermodynamic simulations and prior experimental studies to support the feasibility of obtaining a stable triple-phase microstructure; included a discussion of controlling grain growth during annealing.

candidates.hypothesis: Introducing alloying elements that promote negative mixing enthalpy—by adjusting the contents of elements such as Al and Ti—in a refractory HEA, followed by controlled low-temperature annealing at 900 °C for 2 hours, will induce sub-nanometer to nanoscale local chemical ordering (LCO) that enhances dislocation cross-slip and work hardening, thereby achieving approximately a 10–15% increase in yield strength and a 10% improvement in ductility, along with a more uniform and higher Young’s modulus compared to a fully random solid solution.
candidates.intervention: Adjust the alloy composition by increasing the content of negative enthalpy promoting elements (e.g. modifying Al and Ti content within a targeted range determined by thermodynamic simulation) and then subject the alloy to low-temperature annealing at 900 °C for 2 hours in an inert atmosphere to induce local chemical ordering without triggering full-scale precipitation.
candidates.changes: Specified the need to adjust alloying elements (such as Al and Ti) quantitatively to target a negative enthalpy window; clarified the processing parameters to favor LCO formation; and added details on advanced characterization methods to quantify the degree of ordering.
